Title: Expanding our partnership with GSA to bring Claude to all levels of government

URL Source: https://www.anthropic.com/news/expanding-partnership-gsa

Markdown Content:
We are expanding our partnership with the General Services Administration (GSA) through a new agreement that gives government partners a 40% discount on Claude Enterprise, Claude for Government, and the Claude API. For the first time, the discount applies across every product surface, including when agencies buy from us directly today and through cloud providers in the coming months. The discount also extends to state, local, tribal and territorial governments.

We are also launching a dedicated program to help agencies implement and make the most of their Claude use. These programs are commonly leveraged by our private sector customers and we’re looking forward to bringing those best practices to our public sector partners in the coming weeks.

Approximately 500 US federal, state, and local government organizations now use Claude. Weekly Claude for Government active users are up about eightfold since February, and usage across federal civilian agencies has grown about 20-fold in a year. Those organizations run some of the most important systems in the country, usually on tight budgets and with long procurement cycles. This agreement is built to support that work, so they can apply Claude to hard problems without a large upfront commitment.

The discounts offered through the agreement are estimated to save the government $1 billion. Agencies are not bound by a minimum spend commitment and will be able to pay for the usage they consume.

### **How Claude is helping public servants get more done**

Government agencies are using Claude to solve some of their most important challenges. Examples include managing backlogs, records and forms, and modernizing old code. Some of the ways agencies are using Claude include:

*   Utah gave Claude Code to 34 developers across 10 state agencies. 80% had a working environment within 30 minutes, 71% reported saving 20+ hours by the end of the four-week pilot.
*   A US state CIO confirmed their team was able to respond to a ransomware attack in 8 minutes vs. the usual 2-3 days thanks to Claude.
*   A US federal security team used Claude Mythos to detect and patch the vulnerability that would have allowed for the takeover of a critical production system in about two days. A human penetration test the month before had missed it.
*   A cybersecurity professional at a major agency found and patched bugs in critical financial systems.
*   A US state IT developer moved nearly 900 API methods to a new framework in two days. The project had been scoped for a month.
*   A US state IT director used Claude Code to document 12 legacy code repositories, mapping 467 database tables and flagging 27 risks along the way.
*   More than half of the US states, some of the largest localities, and some of the countries largest critical infrastructure operators [participated](https://www.anthropic.com/news/anthropic-cyber-mission) in our SLTT cyber defense program.

### **Meeting government security requirements**

Agencies can use Claude for their most sensitive unclassified work. Claude for Government, which delivers Claude's coding and agentic work capabilities and provides near-feature parity with commercial offerings at a FedRAMP High authorization level, was made [generally available](https://claude.com/resources/articles/claude-for-government-is-now-generally-available) on September 30.

Agencies building their own tools can use Claude through Amazon Bedrock or Google Cloud’s Vertex AI. On Bedrock, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High, with select models authorized for DoD IL4 and IL5 workloads in AWS GovCloud. On Vertex AI, Claude is authorized for FedRAMP High.

Claude Enterprise is in process for FedRAMP Moderate authorization through the FedRAMP 20x program, marking the next evolution of how we are bringing the same innovative technology available commercially to the government.

### **Getting started**

Government agencies can buy Claude at the OneGov discount through GSA's Multiple Award Schedule today. Whether your department or agency already uses Claude or is interested in using it, our Public Sector team will help discuss your options.

For more information, contact us [here](https://claude.com/solutions/government).

_Anthropic’s [life sciences team](https://www.anthropic.com/science) is working to accelerate curing disease. Over the past several months, our scientists have engaged in deep research partnerships with six organizations developing new medicines: [BigHat Biosciences](https://www.bighatbio.com/), [Bristol Myers Squibb](https://www.bms.com/), [Divergence Labs](https://divergencelabs.com/), [Enveda](https://enveda.com/), [Generate Biomedicines](https://generatebiomedicines.com/), and [The Column Group](https://www.thecolumngroup.com/). We've also begun drug discovery efforts of our own. In doing so, we've learned a lot about how Claude can support drug development, and how we’ll need to improve Claude further to realize AI's potential in medicine. We plan to scale this work up substantially from here_.

There are many opportunities to speed up drug development, even beyond the most commonly discussed applications of AI, like [proposing initial designs](https://www.anthropic.com/research/Claude-accelerates-protein-design) for new molecules. Developing a drug involves many varied tasks: doing early research to identify a target for a drug and the right type of drug to engage it, designing a molecule with the right properties, optimizing it to be manufactured reliably at scale, drafting the regulatory filings needed to run clinical trials, designing and administering those trials, and much more.

Our strategy to realize AI’s medical benefits is based on having AI increasingly involved in all of these tasks. There is no single problem to solve; the bottlenecks are distributed all throughout the drug development process. The best way to identify and work through these bottlenecks is to get deeply involved in real drug programs, across many different disease areas and stages of development.

So, over the past several months, we’ve partnered with six organizations to do so. We’ve also started drug discovery efforts of our own, including programs for rare childhood forms of muscular dystrophy, where Claude handles much of the scientific and operational work.

This work serves our goals in three ways. First, it lets us better understand the strengths and limitations of our models in relation to a much wider range of drug development tasks (we’ve already prioritized specific improvements to our models based on what we’ve learned so far). Second, these programs can serve as case studies for the wider life sciences community. If Claude is to significantly increase the rate of new cures, we need to work with many more biotechnology firms and integrate Claude more deeply into their development processes. Third, these projects should, if their positive trajectories continue, have direct impact themselves. We’re optimistic that some may result in effective new medicines for the diseases they target, including food allergies, rare childhood diseases, and several forms of cancer.

In this post, we provide an update on our progress with our partners, along with technical reports that describe our thought process, methods, and early results in more detail. We then briefly outline where our work is headed next.

## Case studies

**Generate Biomedicines: modality engineering.** Generate Biomedicines has been working on increasing the usefulness of a cancer treatment known as CAR T-cell therapy. This therapy has historically helped treat blood cell cancers; Generate aims to reengineer it so that it can treat solid tumor cancers too. To do this, they’re aiming to shorten one part of the therapy’s genetic instructions, which would create room for additional instructions suited to other kinds of cancer. Six Generate scientists used Claude Code to propose new designs for this part. One design was about 70% shorter than the standard version, and in lab tests it was more effective: it allowed immune cells to make roughly 10 times as many receptors (the proteins they use to spot cancer cells), it killed tumor cells more efficiently, and the immune cells remained active for longer. Read more, and see [Generate’s technical report](https://generatebiomedicines.com/publications/refactored-intracellular-domains-enhance-car-expression-and-function/).

**Divergence Labs: hit generation.** Divergence Labs is working on a novel way to treat food allergies. Food allergies are set off by a reaction from a molecule called IgE, some of which is attached to our immune cells and some of which floats freely in our blood. Divergence Labs is developing drugs that would detach the IgE from our immune cells entirely, rather than solely neutralizing the IgE circulating in our blood, as standard medications do. This could provide a much more effective treatment, but it requires a precise design, with two “arms”: one that would bind tightly to IgE, and another that would help prise IgE from the immune cell. Claude converted Divergence Labs’ goals into a detailed design plan, and then, largely autonomously, generated roughly 35,000 antibody designs in about a month to be narrowed down and tested. In those early tests, Divergence found “hits” for both arms: three designs that could bind to IgE, and 20 that could dislodge it. Three of those 20 appeared to dislodge IgE more than the standard medication. Its next step is to build a drug that combines the two arms. Read more, and see [Divergence’s technical report](https://divergencelabs.com/publications/ige-preprint.pdf).

**BigHat Biosciences: lead optimization.** BigHat Biosciences pairs AI with an automated lab to improve potential drugs (or “leads”), which must bind their target tightly, remain stable through manufacturing and storage, and avoid clumping together (among other criteria). BigHat’s scientists and an Anthropic researcher worked with Claude to improve these three properties in two leads, both antibody fragments that could become parts of future drugs: one designed to target cancer cells, and one designed to keep a drug in the body longer. Claude, connected to BigHat’s lab data system, Reccy, proposed changes to each molecule, and BigHat’s lab made and tested about 1,010 variants in about 10 weeks. Partway through, the team suspected the standard heat-stability and clumping metrics were misleading. Claude and the researcher reanalyzed the raw data, then proposed different metrics and a protocol change to test them. BigHat’s scientists refined and ran it, and the main predictions held. Compared with the originals, the best versions bound more than 10x more tightly, the cancer-targeting lead stayed in solution 18°C higher, and the lead for longer-lasting drugs clumped more than 100x more slowly. Read more, and see [BigHat’s technical report](https://www.bighatbio.com/bighat-anthropic-collaboration-report-10-27-2026).

**Enveda: manufacturing and filings.** To conduct clinical trials, companies need records showing that each batch of a new drug has been made to strict quality standards, and to submit an application to regulators, among other requirements. At Enveda, manufacturing chemists spent up to 75% of their time on paperwork. To ease the load, Enveda built a system that connects all of its manufacturing documents to Claude, then lets Claude flag any possible issues. Over tests on 1,061 pages of documentation, Claude caught all 11 issues that human reviewers had spotted—and flagged seven they’d missed. In the process, this method reduced human review time by 89%, from over 25 hours to less than three. Separately, Claude wrote the first drafts of two important regulatory documents. One took four hours, compared to about three months by hand. For the other, Enveda’s standard human review process found one minor error. Read more, and see [Enveda’s technical report](https://enveda.com/CMC-Document-Processor/).

**The Column Group (TCG): company creation.** Because drug discovery can be slow, expensive, and prone to failure, investors in biotechnology companies have favored safer, previously validated ideas over riskier new ones, even when the latter could help more patients. We’ve been working with TCG to see whether Claude can change this by cutting the time and cost of drug discovery so that investors can confidently support more ambitious ideas. Specifically, TCG is establishing Pleiades, a new company that will use Claude to run many more—and more complex—drug programs than is usual for a small team. This could be a model for how Claude can reduce both the scientific and the operational and administrative overhead required to run a biotechnology company. If this works, this model could be replicated across the industry and direct investment toward harder problems in medicine. Pleiades is currently developing new tools and workflows for Claude; its very first Claude skill, which helps Claude assess whether drug targets are worth pursuing, has been evaluated on 45 target-disease pairs. Read more.

More recently, we’ve also begun working with [Bristol Myers Squibb](https://www.bms.com/) (BMS) to find and address bottlenecks in clinical trial planning. BMS is using Claude to assess plans of an early-stage drug in clinical trials, and to estimate the likelihood of those trials succeeding. Together, we plan to expand this work in 2027 to understand its potential for increasing the probability of success in early development.

> _“We use Claude at the clinical trial stage to analyze proprietary data, create a clinical study plan, and weigh the study’s chance of success. From a single prompt, Claude generated a robust initial analysis that helped inform our assessment of different development options, which would otherwise take days to complete. We did all of this while ensuring the security of our highly sensitive data. We look forward to expanding this work across our pipeline to support portfolio-level decisions.”_

_**Michael Pourdehnad, MD**, Senior Vice President, Head of Early Clinical Development, Hematology, Oncology and Cell Therapy._

In addition to our work with these partners, we’ve begun to run some research programs ourselves. We’ve acquired Mithril Medicine, a one-person company that has been developing treatments for two rare forms of muscular dystrophy. Its founder, Cody Tranbarger, used Claude to organize contracts, logistics, and experiments with 11 external labs, and delegated many other aspects of Mithril’s operations to Claude. As a result, Mithril took a possible treatment for one form of muscular dystrophy from an idea to promising results in mice in less than 18 months. Now at Anthropic, Cody is continuing this research, and plans to start several new programs. If his drug candidates continue to hold up, we expect a drug to be ready to start clinical trials in humans as soon as late 2028. Read more and see [our technical report](https://www-cdn.anthropic.com/52e1f5d50c47ca3818f56704c27cf19e59b62e77.pdf).

## Extending our work in the life sciences

All of this research is still at an early stage. In particular, so far it is mostly _preclinical—_ that is, for the most part, it isn’t yet at the stage where the drugs are being tested in humans. We plan to continue extending Claude’s role into clinical trials as these drug programs advance, and as we partner with more organizations whose drug development programs are already at the clinical stage.

This research is only one part of our efforts to accelerate drug discovery. Ultimately, we want to share our models with as many drug development researchers as possible. To that end, we’ve rolled out [Claude Science](https://www.anthropic.com/news/claude-science-ai-workbench), our AI workbench for researchers, and we’re providing [Claude credits for life scientists](https://www.anthropic.com/news/ai-for-science-program). We’ve also created the [Life Sciences Verification Program](https://www.anthropic.com/news/life-sciences-verification-program) to allow trusted organizations to use our most powerful models with more permissive versions of our safeguards, which are necessary to prevent misuse but which can impede legitimate biological research. We’ve also recently launched an [open call for guest investigators](https://www.anthropic.com/news/open-call-guest-investigators-life-sciences) in the life sciences; we’re seeking proposals from research groups who want to use Claude to investigate key questions in drug discovery and other areas.

We’re looking forward to working with many more organizations as we expand our life sciences research. If you work at an organization focused on drug discovery and are interested in collaborating with us, you can get in touch below.

## Generate:Biomedicines: Redesigning a component of CAR T-cell therapy

_The Generate:Biomedicines team shares how they worked with Claude to redesign a component of CAR T-cell therapy to make it more compact, freeing up space for new functions that could help treat cancer._

_Read Generate’s [technical report](https://generatebiomedicines.com/publications/refactored-intracellular-domains-enhance-car-expression-and-function/) and get in touch (info@generatebiomedicines.com)._

[Generate:Biomedicines](https://generatebiomedicines.com/) designs protein drug candidates using machine learning and frontier biohardware. Over the past eight months, a six-person team of Generate scientists redesigned a stubborn component of chimeric antigen receptor (CAR) T-cell therapy, a type of cancer therapy, with help from Claude.

CAR T-cell therapy uses genetically engineered versions of patients’ own immune cells to attack cancer cells. The part the Generate scientists redesigned is called the signaling domain—the section of the engineered receptor that tells the immune cell to attack. Making it shorter frees up space for other functions in the CAR’s genetic instructions, such as attacking several cancer markers at once or adding proteins that help the T-cell survive inside a tumor.

Working with Claude and other AI tools, Generate’s scientists built and directed a system of AI agents to design signaling domains that are much more compact than a standard version used in several approved therapies. The best design was about 70% shorter and no less effective. In laboratory tests, one of the top designs put roughly 10 times as much receptor on the cell surface—which may make a T-cell better able to recognize and attack cancer cells—and the lead designs killed tumor cells more efficiently than the standard version.

*   _Read Generate:Biomedicine’s technical report, “[Refactored intracellular domains enhance CAR expression and function](https://generatebiomedicines.com/publications/refactored-intracellular-domains-enhance-car-expression-and-function/).”_

### Why improving CAR T-cell therapy is a challenge

CAR T-cell therapy has transformed the treatment of several blood cancers, but the drugs themselves are cumbersome to manufacture. Today, a patient’s T-cells are removed, engineered in a factory over several weeks, and infused back into the patient. A major goal for the field is to do that work _inside_ the body: delivering the genetic instructions for building the receptor directly to the patient’s T-cells. This could be a faster and cheaper way to deliver the therapy and could expand what CAR T-cell therapy can do. In particular, it could make the therapy better suited to treating autoimmune conditions, as well as early-stage solid tumor cancers, against which it has so far been less successful.

But delivering genetic instructions into a living cell means working within tight constraints. Space is at a premium: the instructions are typically delivered either by a viral vector or a lipid nanoparticle carrying mRNA, both of which can only hold a limited amount of genetic material. It would be helpful to give the CAR more functions, or to bundle in protective proteins to help the T-cell survive inside a tumor. The more compact each part of the receptor is, the more room is left in the delivery vehicle for these extra functions.

One way of boosting a CAR’s functionality would be to improve the delivery system—for example, by designing a capsule that can carry more genetic instructions. To use a software analogy, it would be like making a larger flash drive that can carry more information. 🚀 Mistral AI’s Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3 ranks #2 out of 9 models by DER on Voice Arena’s Diarization + ASR leaderboard, outperforming its larger counterpart.

Following the launch of Mistral’s new Voxtral 3 family, we evaluated its Mini and Small transcription models on Voice Arena’s Diarization Bench.

🥈 Voxtral Mini Transcribe 3: 40.4% DER (#2)
Voxtral Small Transcribe 3: 41.1% DER (#4)

Both models were tested on 139 held-out conversations under identical conditions, using human-verified references, a strict 0 ms collar, and no predefined speaker counts or audio cleanup.

Mini leads on in-person conversations (40.6% vs. 41.5%), while Small performs slightly better on online calls (39.1% vs. 39.5%).

Overlapping speech remains the biggest challenge. Missed speech accounts for 82% of Mini's total DER. Both models correctly identify the exact number of speakers in 83.5% of sessions.

Congratulations to @MistralAI on the release ! 👏 

View complete track & condition breakdown: https://t.co/sLGwgH3EWt

article.description:
We’ve trained Claude to flag potential misuse in conversations, a technique we call self-assessment. Right after it responds, Claude gives a preliminary safety assessment of the conversation. 

Since we began using self-assessment in June, it has surfaced misuse that our other safeguards weren’t designed to catch. 

Because Claude has already read the conversation, self-assessment is very efficient. And unlike classifiers, which target a discrete set of harms, it draws on Claude’s own judgment, so it gets more accurate as our models improve.

Read more on our new Safeguards blog:
https://t.co/18j6zdHub4

article.title:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since th
article.description:
Today, we’re sharing a look at our expanded system for monitoring frontier models at OpenAI, which in September helped us catch a model’s attempt to access the live internet during training.

Since the Hugging Face incident—when models broke out of an internal cybersecurity investigation where we weren’t running our misalignment monitors—we’ve substantially expanded our monitoring of frontier agents. We now monitor all frontier reinforcement learning runs and evaluations, as well as all internal Codex use. When our system finds evidence of a problem that might require intervention, it rapidly alerts human responders who can investigate and take action.

To detect when a model’s behavior departs from what we intended, we use several layers of monitoring. Activation probes look for patterns in a model’s internal activity. Reviewer models examine its reasoning and tool use, and investigative agents can read back through the model’s entire transcript to understand how a sequence of actions fits together and whether it warrants human review.

To test whether our current system would have detected the Hugging Face incident, we replayed the recorded activity with our new monitors in place. In the replay, our monitors alerted our security team about 30 minutes after the agents escaped their sandbox. That was more than 30 hours before the point at which the agents breached Hugging Face’s systems in the original incident.

In September, a model exploited a DNS misconfiguration to reach the live internet. Our monitors flagged the breach within 15 minutes, and a responder began reviewing the alert three minutes later. The alert enabled responders to investigate while the run was still underway.

As we give models more autonomy, we need to know when they cross a boundary we expected to hold. We believe that monitoring is essential to catching those failures in time for people to intervene. 
https://t.co/dIYP7B1GlD

article.title:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate
article.description:
New Anthropic research: Automating subtle emergent misalignment research.

Red-teaming is a vital part of model safety testing, but it’s also limited by researchers’ time. To see if we could automate it, we set thousands of Claude agents the task of evading a training data monitor.

These agents developed training data that looked harmless to monitors (like a veteran wrestler mentoring a newcomer, or a Q&A about professional beekeeping), but that in fact taught misaligned behavior.

Examples like these can be used to directly improve future training data monitors. This research is only a first step, but it suggests that future red-teaming efforts could improve much further, using better models and more compute.

Read the full post on the Alignment Science Blog: https://t.co/24Gs1oSw7Q

article.title:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to veri
article.description:
New Anthropic research: progress on provable inference for large language models.

Here, we introduce FlashProve. Building on established cryptographic techniques, FlashProve allows developers to verify whether a given response came from a given AI model. It’s substantially more efficient than prior open-source methods for doing so. 

These proofs have a range of applications. They can, for instance, make it harder for attackers to hijack a chat, or enable safety evaluators to verify that the model they’re testing is the same one being served to customers.

For our full write-up, see here: https://t.co/OIZWPb6QZa

Further progress in provable inference will likely be an important part of improving trust in AI deployment. To that end, we're open-sourcing FlashProve’s code, here: https://t.co/7ky3Ir8V06

We’re grateful to our collaborators: Alessandro Chiesa, @GiacomoFenzi, @gwberg95, @miranda__christ, Rahul Dalal (https://t.co/pjWKLHWXyz) and Ben Mayer (@transmissions11).
